Run a `/grilling` session.


ARGUMENTS: Imagine you are coming back from lunch and you see 8 agents requiring your attention.
Which one should you look into first? This is what Plane Sight is trying to help you decide.

Your product development is like an airport. Agents are taking off from the terminal, spin their engines and generate trails before they land again. To prevent any unnecessary delays, a short turnaround time is crucial.

Plane Sight acts as your air traffic controller. It hides agents which are in-flight, because they are not actionable. It recognizes the most urgent task in front of the line and identifies dependencies between agents, so they don’t collide.

In our control tower sits our operator is Gemini 3.8 Flash, which sees all of your agent sessions from above and lines them up in the right order of priority.

On the ground control we have Herdr, which takes command from our operators and leads the agents the right way.

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled — the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Each question should be formatted like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree — settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent to find it — don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report — ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's — put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

input.description: List repo files and show the README

input.prompt:
Find out what "Herdr" is. It is likely a developer tool for running or managing multiple AI coding agent sessions (for example Claude Code, Codex) — possibly a terminal multiplexer, CLI or desktop app. Check the web (search "herdr agents", "herdr github", "herdr cli") and also check whether it is installed locally (`which herdr`, `brew list | grep -i herdr`, `ls ~/.herdr ~/.config/herdr 2>/dev/null`, `herdr --help`).

Report concisely:
1. What Herdr is, its homepage/repo URL, and its current version.
2. Which agent CLIs it supports.
3. Its integration surface: CLI commands, API, socket, hooks, plugin system, config files. In particular: can an external program (a) list all agent sessions and their state (running / waiting for input / done / error), (b) read a session's transcript or recent output, (c) send input or commands to a session, (d) reorder, focus or hide sessions in its UI?
4. Whether it already has any notion of session status, notifications or prioritisation.
5. Whether it is installed on this machine, and the output of its help command if so.
Do not modify anything. Keep the report under 400 words and cite URLs.
